title: 1 Chronicles 2:18–41
context: The list now follows other branches of Hezron besides the Ram-to-David line already given. Caleb the son of Hezron, his wives Azubah, Jerioth, and later Ephrath, and their children, including Hur and Bezalel, stand first. Bezalel, son of Uri son of Hur, is the name also borne by the craftsman of the tabernacle in Exodus; the identification is commonly made and may be noted, but this verse-group does not retell Exodus and should not be pressed beyond the names. Hezron’s later marriage into the house of Machir, father of Gilead, and the towns of Jair, with a notice that Geshur and Aram took towns of Jair, are given as history in the family record; site identifications should remain modest. After Hezron’s death in Caleb Ephrathah, Abijah bears Ashhur, father of Tekoa. The chapter then traces Jerahmeel, Hezron’s firstborn, through several generations, including sons who die without children, and then the line of Sheshan, who has daughters only and gives a daughter to Jarha, his Egyptian servant, from whom a long father-to-son chain runs down to Elishama. Some of these names appear only here. The Chronicler is still working within Judah’s families, not yet closing the royal line, which has already been carried to David in 2:10–15. Both traditions refuse to allegorize the marriages, the servant, or the long list of little-known sons, and they do not force every Caleb or every “father of” a place into a single, certain identification.

verses.text: Caleb the son of Hezron became the father of children by Azubah his wife, and by Jerioth; and these were her sons: Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon.
verses.arminianNotes:
Caleb the son of Hezron has children by Azubah his wife and by Jerioth; her sons are Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon. This Caleb is called son of Hezron, the brother named in 2:9 as Chelubai, a connection often suggested and still to be handled with care. The verse is a family notice, not a map.

Arminian readers take the names as a real household in Judah, without turning the two women or the three sons into types.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hedge the relation of this Caleb to Chelubai and to the Caleb of later verses. The Chronicler is recording Hezron’s line beyond Ram, not writing a parable.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.

verses.text: Azubah died, and Caleb married Ephrath, who bore him Hur.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Azubah died, and Caleb married Ephrath, who bore him Hur.” A second marriage follows a death. Hur will be the father of Uri in the next verse. The name Ephrath is close to the place-name Ephrathah later in the chapter; the verse itself names a wife, and that limit should be kept.

Arminian readers hear an ordinary succession of marriage and birth, a historical note rather than a symbol of the land.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise keep Ephrath as the wife named here, without deciding every later place-name by this line alone.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.

verses.text: Hur became the father of Uri, and Uri became the father of Bezalel.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Hur became the father of Uri, and Uri became the father of Bezalel.” The three-generation chain matches the parentage of Bezalel the tabernacle craftsman in Exodus (for example Exodus 31:2), a commonly noted identification. This verse does not retell that work; it only gives the names.

Arminian readers may acknowledge the Exodus parallel while still reading the line as a Judahite genealogy, not as an allegory of worship.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also name the Exodus Bezalel as a possible and common identification, without forcing this short verse to carry that whole story.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.

verses.text: Afterward Hezron went in to the daughter of Machir the father of Gilead, whom he took as wife when he was sixty years old; and she bore him Segub.
verses.arminianNotes:
Afterward Hezron, at sixty, takes the daughter of Machir, father of Gilead, as wife, and she bears Segub. Machir and Gilead belong to Manasseh’s house in the earlier books; the marriage is a link across tribes, stated as fact. The woman’s own name is not given.

Arminian readers take the age, the marriage, and the birth as historical notes, not as a type of later unions.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same cross-family link. The Chronicler records Hezron’s late marriage into Machir’s house and the birth of Segub, without further comment.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.

verses.text: Segub became the father of Jair, who had twenty-three cities in the land of Gilead.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Segub became the father of Jair, who had twenty-three cities in the land of Gilead.” Jair’s cities are numbered; their exact sites are not listed here, and identifications should remain modest. The next verse will add a further notice about towns of Jair.

Arminian readers take the twenty-three cities as a real holding in Gilead, recorded in a family list, not as a coded geography.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also decline to map each city from this verse alone. Jair, son of Segub, had twenty-three cities in Gilead, as the text says.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.

verses.text: Geshur and Aram took the towns of Jair from them, with Kenath, and its villages, even sixty cities. All these were the sons of Machir the father of Gilead.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Geshur and Aram took the towns of Jair from them, with Kenath, and its villages, even sixty cities. All these were the sons of Machir the father of Gilead.” A loss of towns is recorded, and the count rises to sixty with Kenath and its villages. The political history is stated in one sentence; it should not be expanded into a campaign the verse does not describe.

Arminian readers keep the notice as a brief historical memory inside the genealogy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same plain report. Towns associated with Jair were taken by Geshur and Aram; the list then ties these names back to Machir.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.

verses.text: After Hezron died in Caleb Ephrathah, Abijah, Hezron’s wife, bore him Ashhur the father of Tekoa.
verses.arminianNotes:
After Hezron died in Caleb Ephrathah, “Abijah, Hezron’s wife, bore him Ashhur the father of Tekoa.” The phrase “father of Tekoa” may mark Ashhur as ancestor or clan-head of that place; the identification of every later town named Tekoa should not be pressed as certain from this line alone.

Arminian readers take the death, the wife, and the birth as family facts, without allegorizing the place-name.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hedge the force of “father of” a town. The Chronicler records Ashhur, born after Hezron’s death, in connection with Tekoa.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.

verses.text: The sons of Jerahmeel the firstborn of Hezron were Ram the firstborn, Bunah, Oren, Ozem, and Ahijah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jerahmeel, firstborn of Hezron, has sons: Ram the firstborn, Bunah, Oren, Ozem, and Ahijah. This Ram is Jerahmeel’s son, not the Ram of 2:9–10 through whom David’s line was traced. The two names should be kept distinct unless the text itself merges them, which it does not do here.

Arminian readers receive a second Ram in Hezron’s house, a real firstborn of Jerahmeel, not a duplicate to be erased.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse to collapse the two Rams. The Chronicler is now following Jerahmeel’s own branch, beginning with his firstborn.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.

verses.text: Jerahmeel had another wife, whose name was Atarah. She was the mother of Onam.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Jerahmeel had another wife, whose name was Atarah. She was the mother of Onam.” A second wife is named, and her son Onam will be followed in a later verse.

Arminian readers take the second marriage as a family fact in the genealogy, not as a moral tale or a symbol.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same plain notice. Atarah is another wife of Jerahmeel, and she is the mother of Onam, whose sons will be listed.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.

verses.text: The sons of Ram the firstborn of Jerahmeel were Maaz, Jamin, and Eker.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The sons of Ram the firstborn of Jerahmeel were Maaz, Jamin, and Eker.” The verse repeats that this Ram is Jerahmeel’s firstborn, and it names three sons otherwise unknown in the narrative books.

Arminian readers let little-known names stand as a genuine record, without inventing stories for Maaz, Jamin, and Eker.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also decline to fill the silence. The Chronicler is still inside Jerahmeel’s house, counting the sons of his firstborn.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.

verses.text: The sons of Onam were Shammai and Jada. The sons of Shammai: Nadab and Abishur.
verses.arminianNotes:
Onam’s sons are Shammai and Jada; Shammai’s sons are Nadab and Abishur. The line of Atarah’s son is now opened, still in Jerahmeel’s family.

Arminian readers take the two generations as historical links, not as a pattern to be allegorized.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear a straightforward continuation of the Jerahmeelite register, moving from Onam to his grandsons.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.

verses.text: The name of the wife of Abishur was Abihail; and she bore him Ahban and Molid.
verses.arminianNotes:
Abishur’s wife is Abihail; she bore him Ahban and Molid. The woman’s name is preserved along with the two sons.

Arminian readers note that the genealogy includes wives when it has them, a record of a household rather than a list of males only at this point.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take Abihail, Ahban, and Molid as names kept because they belong to this family, not because they hide a type.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.

verses.text: The sons of Nadab: Seled and Appaim; but Seled died without children.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nadab’s sons are Seled and Appaim, “but Seled died without children.” The line through Nadab will have to run, if it continues, through Appaim. The death without children is stated without comment.

Arminian readers hear a real end of one branch, a historical blank, not a judgment scene invented from silence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers keep the same restraint. Seled died without children; Appaim remains, and the next verse will follow him.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.

verses.text: The son of Appaim: Ishi. The son of Ishi: Sheshan. The son of Sheshan: Ahlai.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The son of Appaim: Ishi. The son of Ishi: Sheshan. The son of Sheshan: Ahlai.” The line reaches Sheshan and Ahlai. Verse 34 will say that Sheshan had only daughters.

Arminian readers leave the two notices to be read together in the verses that follow.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise refuse a forced solution. The register names Ahlai after Sheshan, and a later verse will say Sheshan had only daughters.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory.

verses.text: The sons of Jada the brother of Shammai: Jether and Jonathan; and Jether died without children.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jada, brother of Shammai, has sons Jether and Jonathan; “Jether died without children.” As with Seled, a branch ends, and the next verse will follow Jonathan.

Arminian readers take the second childless death as another historical note in Jerahmeel’s house, not as a moral to be drawn without the text.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same spare fact. Jether died without children; Jonathan remains to carry Jada’s line in the next verse.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.

verses.text: The sons of Jonathan: Peleth and Zaza. These were the sons of Jerahmeel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan’s sons are Peleth and Zaza. “These were the sons of Jerahmeel.” The formula closes the Jerahmeelite section before the special notice about Sheshan.

Arminian readers receive Peleth and Zaza as the last named sons in this branch, and the summary as the Chronicler’s own close of Jerahmeel’s house so far.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the summary at face value. The sons of Jerahmeel have been traced through several generations, and the list now pauses to explain Sheshan’s family.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.

verses.text: Now Sheshan had no sons, but only daughters. Sheshan had a servant, an Egyptian, whose name was Jarha.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now Sheshan had no sons, but only daughters. Sheshan had a servant, an Egyptian, whose name was Jarha.” This sits beside Ahlai’s being named in verse 31. The next verse records a daughter given to Jarha.

Arminian readers let both notices stand. Some suggest that Ahlai is that daughter, a common reading that should remain hedged.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also decline to erase verse 31 or verse 34. The Chronicler states that Sheshan had only daughters and that he had an Egyptian servant, Jarha.

Both traditions keep this as family history, and they treat the identification of Ahlai with the daughter in verse 35 as a possibility, not a certainty.

verses.text: Sheshan gave his daughter to Jarha his servant as wife; and she bore him Attai.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Sheshan gave his daughter to Jarha his servant as wife; and she bore him Attai.” The daughter’s own name is not given. The line will continue through Attai in a long father-to-son chain. The marriage is recorded, not moralized.

Arminian readers hear a historical arrangement in the household, a daughter given to the Egyptian servant, and a son born. Some identify her with Ahlai in verse 31, though the text does not say so.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers keep the same restraint. The genealogy proceeds through this marriage to Attai, a fact of Sheshan’s house rather than a type.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.

verses.text: Attai became the father of Nathan, and Nathan became the father of Zabad,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Attai became the father of Nathan, and Nathan became the father of Zabad,” Two steps begin a chain of otherwise little-known names. This Nathan is not identified by the verse with Nathan the prophet or with David’s son Nathan, and such identifications should not be assumed.

Arminian readers take the two births as links in Sheshan’s recorded line, nothing more.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse to merge this Nathan or Zabad with better-known men of the same names. The list is still in Jerahmeel’s wider family.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.

verses.text: and Zabad became the father of Ephlal, and Ephlal became the father of Obed,
verses.arminianNotes:
“and Zabad became the father of Ephlal, and Ephlal became the father of Obed,” The chain continues, still without stories attached to the names.

Arminian readers let Ephlal and this Obed stand as historical links, not as the Obed of Ruth unless the text says so, which it does not.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise keep the names in their own list. The Chronicler is counting descent, not writing a second Ruth genealogy here.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.

verses.text: and Obed became the father of Jehu, and Jehu became the father of Azariah,
verses.arminianNotes:
“and Obed became the father of Jehu, and Jehu became the father of Azariah,” Again the verse is only a pair of births. This Jehu and this Azariah are not identified with the king or the priest of those names.

Arminian readers refuse to pull later famous figures into a list that does not name them as such.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave Jehu and Azariah as men of this genealogy, without a forced identification with other bearers of the names.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.

verses.text: and Azariah became the father of Helez, and Helez became the father of Eleasah,
verses.arminianNotes:
“and Azariah became the father of Helez, and Helez became the father of Eleasah,” The register moves on two more steps, still in the same style.

Arminian readers take Helez and Eleasah as further historical names in Sheshan’s line, unnarrated and unallegorized.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same continuation. The Chronicler’s interest here is descent, name after name, down a Judahite branch.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.

verses.text: and Eleasah became the father of Sismai, and Sismai became the father of Shallum,
verses.arminianNotes:
“and Eleasah became the father of Sismai, and Sismai became the father of Shallum,” Two more otherwise obscure names are added. This Shallum is not identified by the verse with later kings or officers of that name.

Arminian readers keep Sismai and Shallum inside this family list, without borrowing a story from another Shallum.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also decline those identifications. The chain is still running from Attai toward its close in the next verse.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.

verses.text: and Shallum became the father of Jekamiah, and Jekamiah became the father of Elishama.
verses.arminianNotes:
“and Shallum became the father of Jekamiah, and Jekamiah became the father of Elishama.” The long chain from Jarha and Sheshan’s daughter ends at Elishama. The name is shared with other men in Scripture; this verse does not say which, if any, later Elishama is in view.

Arminian readers take the close as the end of this recorded line, a historical stop, not a coded climax.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise leave Elishama as the last name in this unit, without forcing a well-known identification. The Jerahmeelite and Sheshan material has been traced as far as the Chronicler takes it here.

Both traditions keep this as family history inside Judah, not as allegory, and they do not invent contrasts over names, skipped generations, or uncertain identifications.
